questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(90,49)$.
What are the mean and the standard deviation of $X$?

options.why: Read the second number as the standard deviation, but it is the variance.
Swapped the two entries, taking the variance as the mean.
Took the square root correctly but then swapped it with the mean.

questions.question_text:
A normal random variable $T$ has mean $15$ and standard deviation $0.2$.
Which notation describes $T$?

options.why: Wrote the standard deviation in the position that holds the variance.
Wrote the variance first and the mean second.
Reversed the order and also used the standard deviation instead of the variance.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the standard normal distribution?

options.why: Wrote the two entries in the wrong order, giving a variance of $0$, which no normal curve can have.
Has mean $0$, but its standard deviation is $\sqrt{2}$ rather than $1$.
Has standard deviation $1$, but its mean is $1$ rather than $0$.

questions.solution_text:
A distribution is standard normal only when the mean is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$.
In $N(0,1)$ the mean is $0$ and the variance is $1$, so $\sigma=\sqrt{1}=1$.
The standard normal distribution is $Z\sim N(0,1)$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(200,64)$.
Which probability about the standard normal variable $Z$ is equal to $P(X>216)$?

options.why: Found the correct $z$ value but reversed the inequality.
Computed $\frac{200-216}{8}$, subtracting the score from the mean instead of the other way round.
Subtracted in the wrong order and also reversed the inequality.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(140,100)$.
What are the mean and the standard deviation of $Z=\frac{X-140}{10}$?

options.why: Gave the mean and standard deviation of $X$ instead of those of $Z$.
Applied the subtraction of the mean but not the effect of dividing by the standard deviation.
Applied the division by the standard deviation but not the subtraction of the mean.

questions.solution_text:
The standard deviation of $X$ is $\sqrt{100}=10$, so $Z=\frac{X-140}{10}$ is the standardised score.
Subtracting $140$ moves the centre to $0$, and dividing by $10$ shrinks every distance from the centre by a factor of $10$.
The mean of $Z$ is $0$ and its standard deviation is $1$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(48,25)$ and $Y\sim N(300,400)$.
Which pair of scores standardises to the same $z$ value?

options.why: Stepped $X$ by $Y$'s standard deviation $20$ instead of its own $5$, so $x=48+2\times 20=68$ gives $z=4$ while $y=340$ gives $z=2$.
Stepped $Y$ by $X$'s standard deviation $5$ instead of its own $20$, so $y=300+5=305$ gives $z=0.25$ while $x=58$ gives $z=2$.
Swapped the two standard deviations, stepping $X$ by $20$ and $Y$ by $5$, which gives $z=4$ for $X$ and $z=0.25$ for $Y$.

questions.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{25}=5$.
$z$
$=\frac{58-48}{5}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{400}=20$.
$z$
$=\frac{340-300}{20}$
$=2$
The pair $x=58$ and $y=340$ standardises to the same $z$ value.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(-6,3^{2})$.
What are the mean and the standard deviation of $X$?

options.why: Evaluated $3^{2}$ and read the answer as the standard deviation rather than the variance.
Dropped the negative sign on the mean, although a normal mean may be negative.
Took the base of the square as the mean and its value as the standard deviation.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$.
The score $x=58$ standardises to $z=1.5$ and the score $x=34$ standardises to $z=-0.5$.
What are $\mu$ and $\sigma$?

options.why: Found $\sigma$ correctly but then took the mean as the midpoint of $58$ and $34$.
Set the difference of the scores equal to $\sigma$ instead of to $2\sigma$.
Took the midpoint of the scores as the mean and their difference as the standard deviation.

questions.solution_text:
$58=\mu+1.5\sigma$
$34=\mu-0.5\sigma$
Subtracting the second equation from the first removes $\mu$.
$24=2\sigma$
$\sigma=12$
$\mu$
$=34+0.5\times 12$
$=40$

questions.question_text:
“a normal distribution with a mean of 20 and a standard deviation of 10”
Translate the above statement into mathematical notation.

options.why: Uses the standard deviation as the second parameter instead of its square.
Takes a square root even though the given standard deviation is already 10.
Swaps the mean with the variance and also uses the wrong second value.

questions.solution_text: The notation $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ uses the mean first and the variance second. Here $\mu=20$ and $\sigma^2=10^2=100$, so the distribution is $N(20,100)$.

questions.question_text: The standard normal distribution $Z$ is given by…

options.why: A standard normal has mean zero and variance one.
This denotes a general normal distribution, not the standard form.
Its mean is one rather than the required standard mean of zero.

questions.solution_text: A standard normal distribution has mean $0$ and variance $1$. Therefore its notation is $N(0,1)$.
